body.x: The nikah nama is the written record of the marriage contract — the document that says who married whom, on what terms, before which witnesses, on what day. Couples sign it in a blur of celebration and then, often, never read it again. That is a mistake. This is the one document from the wedding that can matter ten or twenty years later, in matters from a wife claiming her mahr to a couple proving their marriage to an embassy. What follows walks through the document section by section, in general terms: forms differ considerably by country, and the Pakistani printed nikah nama, an Indian mosque-issued certificate and a UK community certificate do not look alike. The anatomy, however, is shared.
The opening sections: names, identities and the parties

Every nikah nama begins with identification: the full names of the bride and groom, their fathers' names, ages or dates of birth, addresses and, in many forms, identity document numbers. This section protects everyone against the oldest documentary problem in marriage — ambiguity. Names should match official documents exactly, including spellings, because a mismatch here becomes a headache when the certificate is later produced for a passport, a visa or a bank. The form also records the place and date of the nikah and the name of the person who officiated. Before signing, both families should read this part slowly: it is unglamorous, and it is where nearly all correctable errors live.
The mahr section: prompt, deferred and total

The heart of the document is the mahr entry. Forms typically divide it into the prompt portion (mu'ajjal), payable on demand at or soon after the nikah, and the deferred portion (mu'akhkhar), payable at an agreed later point — classically on dissolution of the marriage or the husband's death, or whenever the wife lawfully demands it according to the contract's terms and applicable rulings. Some forms state a single total figure with the split beneath it; some also record whether any part was actually paid at the ceremony and how. What this section protects is the wife's financial right in black and white: the figure in this box, not the figure anyone remembers being discussed, is the mahr. Agree it before the day, write it unambiguously — in words as well as numerals where the form allows — and never leave it blank or vague on the assumption that it can be sorted out later.
The conditions section: the most skipped, the most significant

Most printed forms include a section for special conditions agreed by the parties, and at most weddings it is left empty — sometimes from contentment, sometimes because nobody explained it. Conditions written here and accepted become part of the contract: agreements about residence, education, work, or other lawful arrangements the couple has genuinely settled. Two cautions matter. First, a condition belongs here only if both sides truly agree to it; the ceremony is not the place to introduce new terms. Second, some pre-printed forms historically contained standard clauses — including, in Pakistan, a clause about delegated divorce — that are sometimes struck through at the ceremony. Never allow a clause to be crossed out without understanding what it says and agreeing to its removal; ask the officiant to explain any printed clause in plain language before anyone signs. If your agreed conditions do not fit the printed space, they can be recorded on a signed annexure with the officiant's help.

Where the bride or groom has appointed a representative (wakil) to recite the contract on their behalf, the form records the wakil's name and the fact of authorisation — this is the paper trail of consent. The signature section then gathers the bride, the groom, the representatives and the officiant. Signatures should be the signer's usual signatures, made in the same sitting wherever possible. This section protects the authenticity of the whole document: it is the answer to any later claim that the marriage did not happen, or happened on different terms. If the bride is signing from a separate room, as happens in many ceremonies, ensure the document that reaches her is the same document, fully filled, and that she or her representative has had the mahr and conditions sections read to her before she signs.

The witnesses' names, identity details and signatures follow. In Shia fiqh witnesses are not a condition of the contract's religious validity, but on paper they are the human evidence of the event, and civil systems lean on them heavily. Choose witnesses who are identifiable and contactable in the future, not merely honoured names. The officiant's signature and stamp then attest that the contract was recited in his presence in the form recorded. If a scholar recited the aqd, his details here connect the religious act to the written record — keep them legible.
Registration notes: the religious record and the state's record

The final sections of many forms deal with registration — the entry of the marriage in a mosque, union council or registrar's records, with a registration number and date. This is where the religious document meets the state, and the relationship between the two differs sharply by country. In Pakistan, the registered nikah nama is itself the official marriage document. In India, practice varies by state and community institution. In the United Kingdom, a nikah performed there is not, by itself, a civil marriage: couples need a separate civil ceremony for the marriage to exist in law, with everything that affects — inheritance, pensions, next-of-kin rights. Whatever your country, ask two questions on the day: where is this marriage being registered, and how do we obtain certified copies? Then obtain them, and store a copy with each family.
Read before you sign: a short checklist

Names and identity details match official documents exactly
The mahr total and its prompt/deferred split are written clearly, not left blank
No printed clause has been struck through without explanation and agreement
Any agreed conditions are written in, or recorded in a signed annexure
Signatures are complete — couple, representatives, witnesses, officiant
You know where the marriage will be registered and how to get certified copies

A nikah nama takes ten unhurried minutes to read. Read it in those ten minutes, and the document will do quietly, for decades, the job it was designed for: proving what two people promised each other, and on what terms.
